title: Genetic Association Studies of Suicidal Behavior: Progress, Methodological Challenges, and Future Directions Over the Past Decade

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Phenotypic Scope of Suicidal Behavior Genetics
subsections.subsection_title: Definitions and nosological boundaries of suicidal behavior
subsections.content:
A central challenge in psychiatric genetics is that “suicidal behavior” is not a unitary phenotype. Contemporary frameworks distinguish suicidal ideation, suicide plans, suicide attempts, and suicide death, while also separating these from non-suicidal self-injury on the basis of inferred intent to die. This distinction is foundational because suicidal thoughts are far more prevalent than attempts, and attempts are only imperfectly predictive of suicide mortality; collapsing these outcomes can therefore obscure etiologic heterogeneity and attenuate genetic signals ref [1], ref [2].

Nosological boundaries are further complicated by the fact that intent, lethality, planning, and medical damage vary continuously across acts of self-harm. Standardized nomenclature has sought to reduce this ambiguity by defining suicide attempt as a non-fatal, self-directed, potentially injurious behavior with at least some intent to die, and suicide as death caused by self-directed injurious behavior with intent to die as a result of the behavior ref [3]. These definitions are especially important in genetic studies, where case ascertainment may rely on clinical interviews, hospital records, death certificates, or biobanks with uneven resolution of intent and method.

For gene-discovery efforts, phenotype definition is therefore not a mere descriptive issue but a source of measurement error and cross-study non-comparability. Broad phenotypes may maximize sample size, but narrower operationalization can better isolate liability dimensions such as progression from ideation to attempt or attempt to suicide death. A clinically informed taxonomy that distinguishes self-harm constructs, while acknowledging their overlap with psychiatric disorders, is essential for interpretable and replicable genetic inference ref [2], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Phenotypic Scope of Suicidal Behavior Genetics
subsections.content:
Clinical heterogeneity is a major obstacle in the genetics of suicidal behavior because “suicidality” often aggregates partially distinct phenomena, including passive death wishes, active ideation, planned attempts, impulsive low-lethality acts, and suicide death. These outcomes differ in prevalence, severity, temporality, and clinical correlates, and evidence from epidemiologic and family studies suggests that transition points within the suicidal process are not interchangeable phenotypes ref [5], ref [6]. As a result, broad case definitions can dilute genetic signal by combining individuals who share only limited liability.

Phenotype refinement therefore aims to reduce etiologic heterogeneity by modeling more homogeneous dimensions of risk. Studies increasingly distinguish attempt from ideation, recurrent from single attempt, medically serious or violent from less lethal behavior, and early-onset from later-onset presentations. Such distinctions are clinically meaningful because attempt characteristics index differing levels of intent, capability, impulsive aggression, and persistence of risk, all of which may map more closely onto underlying biological liability than omnibus definitions ref [7], ref [8]. Structured assessment of intent, method lethality, planning, and repetition is thus essential for cross-study comparability.

A further challenge is that ascertainment context shapes phenotype definition: psychiatric samples enrich for severe comorbidity, whereas population biobanks often rely on self-report items that conflate ideation and behavior. Recent genomic work has shown only partial overlap between the genetics of suicide attempt and related psychiatric disorders, reinforcing the value of refined phenotyping alongside careful adjustment for comorbidity ref [9]. For gene discovery, the central issue is not simply increasing sample size, but increasing phenotype precision.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Phenotypic Scope of Suicidal Behavior Genetics
subsections.content:
Because suicidal thoughts and acts are clinically heterogeneous and relatively low-base-rate outcomes, many studies have turned to endophenotypes and intermediate traits that may index liability more proximally than the distal phenotype itself. In this framework, traits such as impulsive aggression, impaired decision-making, stress responsivity, and altered serotonergic function are attractive because they are measurable across diagnostic categories and may be more stable over time than acute suicidal states. Mann and colleagues proposed a stress-diathesis model in which trait-like deficits in behavioral inhibition and emotion regulation interact with psychiatric illness to increase suicide risk, helping to motivate genetic work on these intermediate phenotypes ref [7].

Among the best studied candidates is impulsive aggression, which has repeatedly been associated with suicide attempt history and is conceptually linked to disinhibition and rapid transition from ideation to action. Neurocognitive impairments in reversal learning, delay discounting, and disadvantageous decision-making have likewise been reported in suicidal patients, suggesting that abnormalities in valuation and cognitive control may represent partially heritable pathways relevant to genetic discovery ref [10]. These measures can sometimes be quantified continuously, improving statistical power and harmonization relative to binary case definitions.

At the same time, the endophenotype strategy has important limitations. Gottesman and Gould emphasized that a valid endophenotype should be associated with illness, heritable, state independent, and cosegregate within families ref [11]; many proposed suicide-related traits only partially satisfy these criteria. Reviews of neurobiological and behavioral correlates of suicidal behavior have therefore argued for caution: intermediate traits may sharpen mechanistic hypotheses, but they are unlikely to map one-to-one onto suicidal outcomes, which emerge from dynamic interactions among genetics, psychopathology, development, and environment ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Phenotypic Scope of Suicidal Behavior Genetics
subsections.content:
Suicidal behavior is strongly embedded within the landscape of psychiatric illness, but it is not reducible to any single diagnosis. Epidemiologic and psychological autopsy studies consistently show that most people who die by suicide meet criteria for at least one psychiatric disorder, particularly mood disorders, substance use disorders, psychotic disorders, and certain personality disorders; however, these disorders are highly prevalent whereas suicidal acts remain comparatively rare, indicating that diagnosis alone has limited specificity for genetic inference ref [13], ref [14]. For genetic studies, this means that case definition must distinguish liability to suicidal behavior from liability to the underlying psychiatric syndrome in which it often occurs.

This distinction is central because genetic associations with suicidal ideation, attempt, or death may reflect shared genetic architecture with major depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, or alcohol use disorder rather than risk specific to suicidal behavior itself. Large-scale molecular studies support substantial overlap between suicide attempt and psychiatric disorders, especially major depression and posttraumatic stress disorder, while also suggesting a partially independent genetic component after accounting for diagnosis ref [9]. Twin and family data similarly indicate both shared familial transmission with psychiatric illness and residual familial effects more specific to suicidal acts ref [15].

Accordingly, studies that ignore psychiatric comorbidity risk conflating pleiotropy, mediation, and phenotype misclassification. More informative designs include within-diagnosis comparisons, adjustment for major psychiatric covariates, and transdiagnostic models that treat suicidal behavior as a correlated but non-identical phenotype. Such approaches are especially important when comparing suicidal ideation with attempts or suicide death, because the degree of overlap with psychiatric disorders may vary across these outcomes ref [9], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Phenotypic Scope of Suicidal Behavior Genetics
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiological significance and public health relevance
subsections.content:
Suicidal behavior is a major public health concern because it combines substantial mortality with a much larger burden of nonfatal morbidity. Global estimates indicate that suicide accounts for more than 700,000 deaths annually and remains among the leading causes of death in adolescents and young adults, underscoring its epidemiological salience across settings ref [17]. This mortality burden is accompanied by far more frequent suicidal ideation and attempts, which generate healthcare utilization, disability, and elevated subsequent risk of suicide death.

From a genetic-epidemiological perspective, public health relevance depends not only on prevalence but also on the strong recurrence and prognostic significance of prior suicidal behavior. Large clinical reviews have shown that a history of suicide attempt is one of the strongest predictors of future suicide, although absolute risk is heterogeneous across populations ref [18]. At the population level, linkage studies further demonstrate that individuals presenting with self-harm or suicide attempt experience markedly increased long-term mortality, including death by suicide and other external causes ref [19].

These epidemiological features make phenotype definition especially consequential for gene discovery. Because suicidal ideation, attempt, and suicide death differ in prevalence, lethality, ascertainment pathway, and demographic patterning, genetic studies that collapse them into a single outcome may obscure biologically informative heterogeneity. Conversely, scalable ascertainment through health systems and biobanks can leverage the public health burden of suicidal behavior to improve power, provided that clinically meaningful distinctions are preserved ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Evolution of Genetic Association Approaches in the Past 10 Years
subsections.content:
Candidate gene association studies occupied a diminishing but still visible role in suicidality genetics during the last decade. These studies typically tested biologically motivated variants in serotonergic, dopaminergic, stress-response, or neurotrophic pathways, extending a literature that had long focused on genes such as SLC6A4, TPH1/TPH2, BDNF, and FKBP5. However, by the 2010s the field increasingly recognized that most early positive findings were based on small samples, heterogeneous phenotypes, and limited correction for multiple testing, conditions that made replication difficult and effect sizes unstable [1, 2].

Meta-analytic and umbrella-style evaluations were especially influential in reframing this literature. Reviews of candidate loci for suicidal behavior found that even the most frequently studied markers showed inconsistent support across cohorts and ancestry groups, with stronger signals often disappearing under stricter evidential standards [1, 3]. This pattern mirrored broader critiques of the candidate-gene era in psychiatric genetics, where biologically plausible hypotheses rarely translated into reproducible associations once adequately powered designs became available [2].

As a result, candidate gene studies are now mainly important for historical context: they shaped early mechanistic thinking and highlighted plausible pathways, but they did not yield robust, standalone markers for suicidal behavior. The methodological lessons from this period—especially the need for large samples, standardized phenotyping, and genome-wide control of false positives—directly motivated the transition toward GWAS, polygenic models, and integrative cross-trait analyses [1, 2, 3, 4].

subsections.section_title: Evolution of Genetic Association Approaches in the Past 10 Years
subsections.content:
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) marked a major methodological break from earlier candidate-gene work by enabling hypothesis-free scans across the genome. In suicidal behavior research, early GWAS were typically underpowered because cohorts were modest and phenotypes were heterogeneous, often combining suicide attempt, suicidal ideation, or completed suicide within psychiatric case-control samples. As a result, initial studies yielded few robust loci and emphasized the need for larger, harmonized consortia and stricter phenotype definition rather than confirming single high-impact variants ref [24], ref [25].

Over the past decade, progressively larger meta-analytic GWAS have begun to detect reproducible common-variant signals for suicide attempt, especially when integrating population biobanks with psychiatric cohorts. These studies also clarified that part of the polygenic liability to suicide attempt is shared with major depression, schizophrenia, and other psychiatric disorders, but that a residual component remains after conditioning on these diagnoses, supporting partial genetic specificity of suicidal behavior itself ref [9], ref [26].

Methodologically, GWAS in this area also exposed persistent challenges: ascertainment differences across clinical versus biobank datasets, ancestry imbalance, and the difficulty of distinguishing risk for suicidal behavior from risk for correlated psychopathology. Nevertheless, the GWAS era shifted the field toward large-scale collaborative science, downstream functional annotation, and integration with cross-trait methods, providing the empirical foundation for later polygenic and multivariate models ref [26], ref [27].

subsections.section_title: Evolution of Genetic Association Approaches in the Past 10 Years
subsections.content:
Polygenic risk score (PRS) analyses were adopted in suicidality research as GWAS summary statistics became available, enabling investigators to test whether aggregate common-variant liability from psychiatric and behavioral traits predicts suicidal ideation, attempt, or death. Early work generally showed that PRS for major depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and related traits explained only a small proportion of variance, but nevertheless provided evidence that suicidal behavior partly reflects diffuse inherited susceptibility shared with broader psychopathology rather than a small number of large-effect loci ref [28], ref [9].

A consistent finding has been the pleiotropic nature of PRS signals. In population-scale analyses, PRS derived from depression and self-harm-related phenotypes were associated with suicidal thoughts and behaviors, but much of the signal attenuated after accounting for psychiatric comorbidity, indicating limited specificity of current scores ref [29]. Relatedly, multivariate genomic analyses have suggested that the genetic architecture of suicide attempt includes both overlap with psychiatric disorders and a residual component not fully captured by them, motivating PRS models that condition on, or jointly model, correlated traits ref [25].

Despite their conceptual value, PRS studies in this field remain constrained by phenotype heterogeneity, modest discovery GWAS size for suicide-related outcomes, and ancestry imbalance. Consequently, predictive performance is still insufficient for clinical use, but PRS analyses have been important in reframing suicidal behavior as a highly polygenic phenotype embedded within a wider network of psychiatric and behavioral genetic risk ref [9], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Evolution of Genetic Association Approaches in the Past 10 Years
subsections.content:
Family-based and linkage-informed designs have occupied a smaller but still important niche in the genetics of suicidal behavior during the past decade. Unlike standard case-control association studies, these approaches leverage within-family transmission, co-segregation, or identity-by-descent sharing to reduce confounding from population stratification and to enrich for variants of larger effect. In psychiatric genetics more broadly, pedigree and family analyses have been particularly useful for parsing the familial aggregation of suicidal behavior from that of correlated disorders such as mood disorders and substance use, while also motivating follow-up molecular analyses in high-risk kindreds ref [30], ref [31].

Evidence from population-based family studies continues to show that suicidal behavior aggregates in families beyond the transmission of major psychiatric illness. In a large Swedish cohort, the familial clustering of suicide was observed even after accounting for psychiatric hospitalization, supporting a partially independent familial liability ref [30]. Twin data have further reinforced a genetic contribution: a meta-analysis of twin studies estimated substantial heritability for suicidal thoughts and behaviors, although with heterogeneity across phenotypes and ascertainment schemes ref [32]. These findings helped justify linkage-informed strategies in multiplex families and genetically informative samples, especially where conventional GWAS remained underpowered for rarer suicidal outcomes.

In practice, however, linkage peaks for suicidal behavior have generally been broad and difficult to replicate, reflecting phenotypic heterogeneity, limited sample sizes, and the likelihood of polygenic rather than Mendelian architecture. Consequently, family-based designs in the last decade have increasingly functioned as complementary frameworks for rare-variant discovery and for testing intergenerational transmission models rather than as stand-alone gene-mapping tools. This shift parallels broader recommendations in psychiatric genetics to integrate pedigree structure with sequencing and registry-based designs to identify higher-risk families and clarify the specificity of inherited liability to suicidal behavior ref [31], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Evolution of Genetic Association Approaches in the Past 10 Years
subsections.content:
Rare-variant work in suicidal behavior has remained comparatively limited, reflecting both the low base rate and phenotypic heterogeneity of suicide attempts and deaths, as well as the large sample sizes required for adequately powered sequence-based analyses. Nonetheless, the move beyond common-variant arrays has been important conceptually: sequencing and exome-focused studies were motivated by the possibility that rare, protein-altering variants of larger effect might help explain risk not captured by genome-wide association studies or polygenic scores.

Early next-generation sequencing efforts were largely exploratory and family- or case-enriched. For example, a whole-exome sequencing study of families with multiple suicide deaths reported rare deleterious variation in biologically plausible neurodevelopmental and synaptic genes, illustrating the potential value of pedigree-based enrichment for identifying uncommon risk alleles ref [34]. Related work in extended Utah high-risk families combined familial ascertainment with sequencing and follow-up analyses, again suggesting that rare functional variants may segregate in a subset of multiply affected pedigrees rather than contributing broadly at the population level ref [35].

More recent studies have shifted toward larger exome resources and aggregate burden testing. In UK Biobank, exome analyses of suicide death or self-harm related phenotypes have generally emphasized gene-based rare-variant burden rather than single-variant discovery, but robust associations specific to suicidal behavior remain sparse compared with findings for other psychiatric outcomes ref [36]. Overall, the sequencing literature has highlighted both promise and current constraints: rare coding variation may be informative in carefully selected families or extreme phenotypes, yet the field still lacks the sample size, harmonized phenotyping, and replication needed to establish reproducible rare-variant signals for suicidal behavior ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Evolution of Genetic Association Approaches in the Past 10 Years
subsections.content:
Cross-trait methods have become important for situating suicidal behavior within the broader genetic architecture of psychiatric illness. Using genome-wide summary statistics, studies increasingly apply linkage disequilibrium score regression, genomic structural equation modeling, and Mendelian-randomization-style frameworks to estimate shared heritability and test whether overlap reflects broad psychopathology or more specific liability dimensions. Large-scale analyses consistently indicate substantial positive genetic correlation between suicide attempt and major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, smoking, insomnia, and other behavioral risk phenotypes, reinforcing the view that suicidal behavior is genetically intertwined with both internalizing and externalizing spectra rather than being an isolated trait ref [9], ref [29].

At the same time, cross-trait analyses have also clarified what remains distinctive about suicidal behavior. In one of the clearest demonstrations, conditioning suicide-attempt GWAS results on major depressive disorder attenuated but did not eliminate the signal, implying a component of genetic liability not reducible to depression alone ref [9]. Related work from the International Suicide Genetics Consortium showed that suicide attempt shares common-variant risk with psychiatric disorders and adverse health-related traits, yet also retains partially independent polygenic architecture ref [25]. These results have encouraged multivariable models that partition shared versus trait-specific effects and have shifted interpretation away from single-disorder explanations.

Methodologically, the main contribution of this literature has been to move the field from simple comorbidity-based inference to formal quantification of shared genetic etiology. However, estimates remain sensitive to phenotype definition, cohort ascertainment, and the conflation of suicidal ideation, attempt, and death. Recent large biobank analyses of self-harm and suicide-related outcomes illustrate both the power and the limitations of these methods: they robustly detect widespread pleiotropy, but causal interpretation remains constrained by measurement heterogeneity and possible horizontal pleiotropy ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Biological Pathways and Recurrent Genetic Signals
subsections.content:
The serotonergic system has been one of the most consistently investigated biological pathways in suicidal behavior, reflecting longstanding evidence that impaired central serotonin turnover is linked to impulsive aggression, affective dysregulation, and suicidal acts. A pivotal biochemical signal is reduced cerebrospinal fluid 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), which has repeatedly been associated with suicide attempts and completed suicide, supporting a trait-like deficit in serotonergic signaling rather than a state marker of acute illness alone ref [39].

Genetic association studies initially focused on core monoaminergic candidates, especially the serotonin transporter and serotonin receptors. The serotonin transporter promoter polymorphism (5-HTTLPR) in SLC6A4 has been widely studied, but findings for suicidal behavior have been heterogeneous and often contingent on psychiatric context or environmental exposure. Meta-analytic evidence nevertheless suggests that variation in serotonergic genes, including SLC6A4, contributes small and inconsistent effects, consistent with a polygenic rather than single-locus architecture ref [40]. Parallel work has implicated receptor-level variation, particularly HTR1A and HTR2A, in some cohorts, although replication has been uneven ref [41].

More broadly, monoamine signaling intersects with other pathways relevant to suicide risk, including stress responsivity and antidepressant treatment response. This is illustrated by evidence that a functional polymorphism in tryptophan hydroxylase 1 was associated with suicidal behavior in early candidate-gene studies, suggesting that serotonin synthesis itself may modulate vulnerability in at least some populations ref [42]. Overall, the serotonergic literature remains biologically compelling, but the field has shifted from isolated candidate variants toward integrative models in which multiple monoaminergic loci, environmental adversity, and downstream circuit effects jointly shape risk.

subsections.section_title: Biological Pathways and Recurrent Genetic Signals
subsections.content:
Stress-response pathways, particularly regulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, are among the most consistently implicated biological systems in suicidal behavior. Genetic and epigenetic studies converge on components that shape glucocorticoid signaling, feedback sensitivity, and adaptation to early-life adversity. In candidate-gene work, variation in FKBP5 has attracted sustained attention because it modulates glucocorticoid receptor function and stress reactivity; gene-by-environment effects involving childhood trauma have been reported for suicidal behavior, supporting a model in which inherited liability interacts with exposure to severe stressors ref [43].

Related evidence comes from studies of the glucocorticoid receptor pathway itself. Altered expression of the NR3C1 co-chaperone machinery and impaired receptor-mediated feedback have been linked to suicide, while postmortem work has shown reduced glucocorticoid receptor expression in brains of suicide victims with histories of childhood abuse, consistent with long-lasting dysregulation of stress-response circuitry ref [44]. Epigenetic findings further support this interpretation: increased methylation of the NR3C1 promoter in hippocampal tissue from suicide decedents exposed to childhood adversity suggests a mechanism by which environmental stress becomes biologically embedded ref [45].

More broadly, these findings fit with clinical and neuroendocrine observations of HPA-axis hyperactivity in a subset of individuals with suicidal behavior. However, effect sizes in common-variant association studies are generally modest, and signals often overlap with depression, PTSD, and trauma-related phenotypes. Current evidence therefore favors a polygenic stress-sensitivity framework rather than a single-gene model, with FKBP5, NR3C1-related regulation, and trauma-linked epigenetic remodeling as recurrent themes ref [43], ref [45], ref [46].

subsections.section_title: Biological Pathways and Recurrent Genetic Signals
subsections.content:
Neurotrophic signaling and synaptic plasticity have been repeatedly implicated in suicidal behavior, particularly through studies of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Candidate-gene association work has focused on the functional Val66Met polymorphism, motivated by its effects on activity-dependent BDNF secretion and memory-related plasticity ref [47]. Although single-variant findings have often been inconsistent across cohorts, this pathway-level signal remains biologically plausible because impaired trophic support could link stress exposure, affective dysregulation, and reduced adaptive plasticity.

Postmortem and peripheral-expression studies provide convergent support for this interpretation. Decreased BDNF expression has been reported in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus of suicide subjects, suggesting that suicidal behavior may occur in the context of broader deficits in neuroplasticity-related gene regulation ref [48]. Complementing this, altered expression of BDNF and its receptor TrkB has also been observed in brains of suicide completers, reinforcing the view that dysregulated neurotrophin signaling is not limited to one transcript or one region ref [49].

These observations fit a wider model in which stress-related molecular changes converge on synaptic remodeling pathways. Reviews of neurobiology and genetics have emphasized that neurotrophic mechanisms interact with serotonergic signaling, HPA-axis activity, and epigenetic regulation, making them more informative as part of multilevel network models than as isolated candidate loci ref [50]. Overall, the literature supports neurotrophic and synaptic-plasticity pathways as recurrent, though not singly determinative, components of genetic liability to suicidal behavior.

subsections.section_title: Biological Pathways and Recurrent Genetic Signals
subsections.content:
Dopaminergic and broader reward-related pathways have been investigated as candidates for suicidal behavior because they regulate motivation, reinforcement learning, impulsive decision-making, and sensitivity to stress. This framework is especially relevant to phenotypes marked by anhedonia, substance misuse, and aggression, which are common clinical correlates of suicide attempts. Early candidate-gene work therefore focused on functional variation in dopamine receptors, transporters, and catabolic enzymes, although effect sizes have generally been modest and findings inconsistently replicated across samples.

Among the most studied loci, the ANKK1/DRD2 region has attracted interest because the TaqIA polymorphism is associated with reduced striatal D2 receptor availability and altered reward processing, providing a plausible bridge between genetic liability and maladaptive behavioral responses under stress ref [51]. Variation in catechol-O-methyltransferase has also been examined in relation to suicidal behavior, with the Val158Met polymorphism hypothesized to influence prefrontal dopamine tone, executive control, and impulsive-aggressive traits; however, meta-analytic evidence indicates heterogeneity across studies and no uniformly robust signal ref [52]. Similar inconsistency has characterized reports for SLC6A3 and other dopaminergic candidates, suggesting that any contribution is likely polygenic and context-dependent rather than driven by single common variants.

A related literature links suicidal behavior to reward-circuit dysfunction at the systems level. Neuroimaging and clinical studies indicate that blunted ventral striatal responses, impaired valuation of future outcomes, and altered mesocorticolimbic connectivity may accompany suicidal ideation and attempts, particularly in mood disorders ref [12], ref [53]. Consistent with this view, a review integrating molecular and circuit findings argued that dysregulation of dopamine-mediated reward and salience processing may contribute to the transition from distress to action, especially when combined with stress sensitization and deficits in cognitive control ref [54]. Overall, current evidence supports dopaminergic involvement as biologically plausible but genetically diffuse, interacting with other pathways rather than emerging as a singular recurrent association.

subsections.section_title: Biological Pathways and Recurrent Genetic Signals
subsections.content:
Inflammatory and immune-related mechanisms have become an important complement to monoaminergic models of suicidal behavior. Genetic findings have not converged on a single high-effect immune locus, but repeated signals in cytokine, acute-phase, and innate immune pathways are broadly consistent with a model in which peripheral and central immune activation modulates stress reactivity, glutamatergic signaling, and frontolimbic circuit function. This pathway-level interpretation is supported by transcriptomic and biomarker work showing altered inflammatory tone in suicidal states, suggesting that common genetic liability may act through regulation of immune responsiveness rather than through disorder-specific variants alone ref [55], ref [56].

Postmortem brain studies provide some of the strongest mechanistic support for this view. In suicidal individuals, microglial and cytokine-related abnormalities have been reported in cortical regions implicated in affect regulation; notably, increased microgliosis in the dorsolateral prefrontal white matter was observed in suicide victims, consistent with neuroimmune activation within circuits relevant to impulsivity and cognitive control ref [57]. Complementing these tissue-level data, meta-analytic evidence indicates elevated peripheral inflammatory markers, especially interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein, in people with suicidal thoughts or acts, although effect sizes are modest and likely moderated by diagnosis, medication exposure, and medical comorbidity ref [58].

Overall, immune findings in suicidality are best understood as polygenic and pleiotropic, overlapping substantially with depression and stress-related psychopathology rather than defining a suicide-specific genetic architecture. For this reason, current evidence favors enrichment analyses and multimodal integration with transcriptomic, methylomic, and biomarker data over isolated candidate-gene claims, while preserving the hypothesis that inflammatory dysregulation identifies a biologically meaningful subgroup with heightened risk under stress ref [56], ref [58].

subsections.section_title: Biological Pathways and Recurrent Genetic Signals
subsections.content:
Neurodevelopmental mechanisms have been implicated in suicidality through genes that shape synapse formation, neuronal maturation, and circuit assembly, although signals have generally been modest and heterogeneous across cohorts. A notable example is the cell-adhesion molecule pathway: genome-wide data have linked variation in neurexin-related loci to suicide-related phenotypes, consistent with the broader view that liability may partly reflect altered development and stabilization of corticolimbic networks involved in impulse control and affect regulation ref [59]. These findings fit with transcriptomic evidence from suicide deaths showing dysregulation of synaptic and developmental programs in prefrontal cortex, suggesting that genetic risk may converge on enduring abnormalities in neural connectivity rather than on a single transmitter system ref [60].

Circadian biology represents another recurring pathway. Large-scale genetic studies of sleep and chronotype have identified robust associations at core clock and circadian-output loci, including variants near ARNTL and other rhythm-regulating genes ref [61]. Epidemiologic and psychiatric-genetic work has further shown that eveningness chronotype and sleep disturbance are associated with elevated suicidal ideation and attempts, supporting a model in which inherited circadian vulnerability interacts with mood dysregulation, stress exposure, and impaired executive control ref [62].

Overall, neurodevelopmental and circadian findings are best interpreted as pathway-level signals that likely modulate risk indirectly through emotional reactivity, cognitive control, sleep timing, and developmental plasticity. Their effects appear unlikely to be specific to suicidal behavior alone, but they may help explain why suicide risk clusters with early-onset psychopathology, disturbed sleep-wake regulation, and persistent deficits in frontolimbic function.

subsections.section_title: Major Advances, Replication Patterns, and Knowledge Gained
subsections.subsection_title: Shifts from single-gene claims to polygenic models
subsections.content:
A major conceptual advance over the past decade has been the retreat from candidate-gene explanations of suicidal thoughts and behaviors toward a polygenic framework. Earlier literature often emphasized small sets of biologically plausible variants in serotonergic, stress-response, or neurotrophic genes, but these findings proved difficult to reproduce across cohorts and designs. The broader critique of candidate-gene research in psychiatry reinforced this shift, showing that historically prominent associations rarely withstood adequately powered tests and that complex behavioral phenotypes are unlikely to be explained by single loci of moderate effect ref [63].

In suicidality research, genome-wide approaches gradually replaced single-gene claims with models of diffuse liability distributed across many common variants. Large analyses of suicide attempt and related phenotypes have shown that SNP-based heritability is modest but non-zero and that polygenic signal overlaps substantially with major psychiatric disorders, especially depression, while still leaving room for partly distinct components of risk ref [9], ref [25]. This has reoriented the field away from searching for one or two "suicide genes" and toward estimating aggregate genetic burden, shared liability, and cross-trait architecture.

The move to polygenic models has also changed evidentiary standards. Studies now prioritize discovery in large biobanks or psychiatric consortia, genome-wide significance thresholds, and external validation of polygenic scores rather than post hoc interpretation of isolated candidate variants. Recent GWAS of suicide attempt illustrate this transition: they identify replicated loci only sporadically, but consistently support a highly polygenic architecture and encourage integration of genomic effects with environmental, clinical, and developmental risk models rather than genetic determinism ref [25], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Major Advances, Replication Patterns, and Knowledge Gained
subsections.subsection_title: Evidence for shared and unique genetic liability
subsections.content:
A consistent finding across the past decade is that genetic liability to suicidal thoughts and behaviors is partly shared with the broader architecture of psychiatric illness, but is not reducible to it. Large-scale genomic analyses have shown substantial positive genetic correlations between suicide attempt and major depressive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, smoking, pain, and related behavioral phenotypes, supporting a model of broad pleiotropic vulnerability rather than disorder-specific causation alone ref [9], ref [29]. This pattern helps explain why suicidal behavior aggregates across diagnostic categories and why family history of multiple forms of psychopathology often marks elevated risk.

At the same time, emerging evidence indicates a partially unique component of liability for suicidal behavior beyond correlated psychiatric risk. Conditioning analyses in population-scale genome-wide association studies suggest that a meaningful proportion of the common-variant signal for suicide attempt persists after accounting for major depression and other psychiatric disorders, implying some genetic influences more proximal to traits such as impulsive aggression, stress responsivity, pain sensitivity, or decision-making under distress ref [9], ref [64]. Findings from multivariate genomic work similarly indicate both shared internalizing/externalizing pathways and residual variance that is more specific to self-harm and suicidal outcomes ref [65].

Overall, the field has moved away from asking whether there is a single 'suicide gene' and toward estimating how partially overlapping liabilities combine across psychopathology, substance use, and behavioral regulation. The main knowledge gain is therefore conceptual: suicidal behavior appears genetically connected to general psychiatric vulnerability, yet not fully explained by it, which supports models that integrate transdiagnostic burden with more specific pathways to attempt and death ref [29], ref [64].

subsections.section_title: Major Advances, Replication Patterns, and Knowledge Gained
subsections.subsection_title: Replication successes and recurring loci or pathways
subsections.content:
A consistent lesson from the last decade is that replication has been stronger at the level of aggregate signal than for early candidate genes. Large genome-wide analyses have repeatedly shown that suicidal thoughts and behaviors are polygenic and that reproducible findings emerge mainly when sample sizes are sufficiently large and phenotypes are harmonized. In particular, population-scale GWAS of suicide attempt identified genome-wide significant loci and demonstrated cross-cohort consistency in SNP-based heritability and polygenic signal, while parallel work on suicide death also detected significant loci in independent ascertainment frameworks, underscoring that at least part of the genetic architecture is recoverable across study designs ref [25], ref [66].

At the level of biological interpretation, the most recurrent pattern has been enrichment in pathways relevant to brain function rather than replication of single high-effect variants. Gene-based and transcriptome-informed analyses have repeatedly implicated neuronal development, synaptic signaling, and cortical and limbic tissue expression, with overlap extending to pathways previously associated with major depressive disorder, impulsivity, and stress-related psychopathology ref [25], ref [9]. This has shifted the field away from isolated serotonergic or stress-axis candidate loci toward distributed neurobiological systems.

Replication has also been clearest for shared liability. Genetic correlation analyses consistently show that suicide attempt shares substantial common variant risk with depression, schizophrenia, ADHD, smoking, and pain-related traits, even though some signal remains after conditioning on psychiatric disorders ref [9], ref [67]. Thus, the most robustly replicated "loci or pathways" are often not disorder-specific markers, but pleiotropic genomic influences concentrated in CNS-expressed genes and behavioral dysregulation pathways, with emerging evidence for a smaller component more proximal to self-harm liability itself ref [67].

subsections.section_title: Major Advances, Replication Patterns, and Knowledge Gained
subsections.subsection_title: Integration with clinical and psychological risk models
subsections.content:
A consistent lesson from psychiatric genetics is that genetic liability to suicidal thoughts and behaviors is unlikely to operate as a stand-alone predictor; rather, it modestly indexes background vulnerability that must be interpreted alongside proximal clinical and psychological risks. Large-scale analyses show that polygenic liability for suicide attempt overlaps with depression, impulsive aggression, substance use, and other psychopathology, supporting integration with multivariable risk models instead of gene-only explanations ref [9], ref [29]. This has shifted the field toward viewing genetic findings as one layer within broader developmental and stress-diathesis frameworks.

Empirically, the incremental predictive value of polygenic scores over established clinical factors remains limited. In veteran and biobank samples, models that add genomic risk to demographic, diagnostic, and electronic health record variables generally yield only small gains in discrimination, reinforcing the continued dominance of prior attempts, mood and substance disorders, trauma exposure, and acute symptom burden in short-term assessment ref [68], ref [69]. These results have tempered early expectations while clarifying where genetics may be most informative: indexing latent liability, stratifying long-term vulnerability, and helping to parse heterogeneity among patients with superficially similar clinical presentations.

At the same time, genetically informed work has contributed conceptually by connecting clinical risk models to transdiagnostic traits such as negative urgency, emotion dysregulation, and impaired stress responsivity. Reviews of suicidal behavior genetics increasingly argue that the most plausible use of genomic information is in combination with psychosocial exposures and intermediate phenotypes, not as a substitute for careful clinical formulation ref [70]. Thus, integration has advanced the field less by producing clinically decisive prediction than by supporting more layered models in which distal inherited liability interacts with psychiatric illness, environmental adversity, and cognitive-affective mechanisms.

subsections.section_title: Major Advances, Replication Patterns, and Knowledge Gained
subsections.content:
Genetic studies have contributed to risk stratification debates less by delivering clinically actionable prediction than by clarifying the limits of genomic information in a low-base-rate, highly heterogeneous outcome. Large biobank analyses show that polygenic liability for suicidal thoughts and behaviors is detectable at the population level, but effect sizes remain modest and are substantially shared with depression, substance use, impulsivity-related traits, and other psychiatric liabilities rather than being highly specific to suicide itself ref [9], ref [71]. This has reinforced the view that genetic data are unlikely to function as a stand-alone screening tool for imminent suicide risk.

At the same time, genomic findings have informed more nuanced stratification frameworks. Work integrating polygenic scores with environmental and clinical variables suggests that genetic liability may modestly improve long-horizon risk discrimination or help characterize etiologic subgroups, especially when combined with psychiatric history and social adversity, but gains are typically incremental and not yet sufficient for routine clinical deployment ref [72]. Reviews of suicide prediction more broadly also emphasize that, even when many predictors are combined, positive predictive value is constrained by rarity, temporal instability, and outcome heterogeneity; these concerns apply with particular force to genetic markers, whose predictive signal is probabilistic and distal rather than proximal ref [73].

Accordingly, the main contribution of psychiatric genomics to risk stratification has been conceptual rather than dispositive: it supports multilevel models in which inherited liability is one component of background vulnerability, useful for research on mechanisms and subgrouping, but currently inadequate for individual-level clinical triage. This has helped shift debate away from genetic determinism and toward whether genomics can be responsibly incorporated into composite, developmentally informed, and context-sensitive prediction models.

subsections.section_title: Major Advances, Replication Patterns, and Knowledge Gained
subsections.subsection_title: Comparative insights across populations and study settings
subsections.content:
Comparative work across populations and study settings has underscored both the promise and the current limits of genetic inference in suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Most large-scale discoveries have come from European-ancestry biobanks and veteran or health-system cohorts, which has improved power but narrowed generalizability. Cross-cohort analyses suggest that polygenic signals for suicide attempt show some consistency across ascertainment contexts, yet prediction and locus transferability attenuate when ancestry, phenotype definition, and comorbidity structure differ, reinforcing concerns already evident in broader psychiatric genetics ref [74], ref [75].

Differences in study setting also matter substantively. Population biobanks tend to identify broad liability shared with depression, substance use, and socioeconomic adversity, whereas clinically enriched samples capture more severe and recurrent phenotypes with heavier burdens of trauma, medical illness, and treatment exposure. In the Million Veteran Program, suicide-attempt GWAS highlighted substantial overlap with major psychiatric and behavioral risk domains, while also illustrating how sex composition, trauma exposure, and ascertainment through electronic health records can shape observed effect sizes and downstream interpretation ref [76].

A recurring comparative insight is therefore methodological as much as biological: heterogeneity in ancestry, recruitment frame, and phenotype construction can masquerade as etiologic difference. Reviews of suicidal behavior genetics have consequently argued that progress depends on multi-ancestry sampling, harmonized definitions spanning ideation, attempt, and suicide death, and explicit tests of portability across community, clinical, and mortality-based datasets ref [77].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Limitations and Sources of Inconsistency
subsections.subsection_title: Small sample sizes and limited statistical power
subsections.content:
A persistent limitation in this literature is the reliance on modest case-control cohorts, which sharply reduces power to detect the small effect sizes expected for complex traits. Underpowered studies are not only more likely to miss true associations, but also to produce unstable and inflated effect estimates among nominally significant findings, thereby contributing to poor reproducibility across samples ref [78]. This problem is especially acute when analyses are further stratified by subtype, sex, or exposure history, because the effective sample size for each comparison becomes very small.

The statistical consequences extend beyond single-marker discovery. Low power interacts with stringent multiple-testing burdens, encouraging selective emphasis on borderline results and candidate findings that rarely survive larger follow-up efforts. Experience from psychiatric and behavioral genetics has shown that many early association signals identified in small samples failed to replicate once adequately powered genome-wide datasets became available ref [79], ref [80]. More generally, theory and empirical review indicate that low-powered fields tend to generate a literature enriched for exaggerated effects and inconsistent directionality, even when some true effects exist ref [81].

Accordingly, progress has depended on large consortia, meta-analysis, and biobank-scale resources that can estimate effects with greater precision and support robust internal and external validation. Without substantial increases in sample size, the field remains vulnerable to false negatives, winner's curse, and apparent heterogeneity that reflects sampling variance more than genuine biological differences.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Limitations and Sources of Inconsistency
subsections.content:
A persistent source of inconsistency is phenotypic heterogeneity across studies. Case definitions often vary from strict diagnostic interviews to self-report, symptom checklists, or electronic health record proxies, each capturing overlapping but non-identical constructs. This problem is especially acute in psychiatry and other complex traits where diagnostic boundaries are porous and symptom dimensions cut across categorical disorders. Large-scale analyses have shown that substantial genetic signal is shared across nominally distinct psychiatric diagnoses, implying that inconsistent operationalization can blur etiologic inference and attenuate replication ref [74], ref [82].

Ascertainment procedures further distort observed associations. Clinic-based samples tend to enrich for more severe, chronic, comorbid, or treatment-seeking individuals, whereas population biobanks often under-represent severe illness and are affected by healthy-volunteer selection. Such recruitment differences can induce collider bias, alter prevalence and comorbidity structure, and make effect estimates non-comparable across cohorts. The non-random participation and disease ascertainment patterns documented in UK Biobank exemplify how selection can systematically bias both epidemiologic and genetic analyses ref [83], ref [84].

These problems limit both discovery and translation. When phenotypes differ in severity threshold, chronicity, informant source, or comorbidity burden, nominally replicated findings may reflect different underlying liabilities. Greater use of harmonized diagnostic instruments, dimensional phenotyping, transparent ascertainment reporting, and sensitivity analyses across recruitment frames is therefore essential to improve interpretability and portability of results ref [85].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Limitations and Sources of Inconsistency
subsections.content:
Population stratification remains a persistent source of false-positive and distorted association signals when allele-frequency differences track ancestry and ancestry is correlated with case ascertainment, environmental exposure, or health-care access. Early candidate-gene and genome-wide studies often relied on self-reported race or limited principal-component adjustment, which can leave residual structure unmodeled, especially in admixed or geographically heterogeneous samples. Methodological work has shown that even subtle structure can bias association estimates if not adequately controlled, and that standard correction strategies are imperfect when recruitment differs across sites or when family and population structure coexist ref [86], ref [87].

An equally important limitation is the overwhelming ancestry imbalance in discovery cohorts. Most common-variant findings and polygenic scores have been derived primarily from European-ancestry datasets, creating reduced portability, attenuated predictive accuracy, and potential miscalibration in underrepresented populations. This problem is not merely a matter of fairness: differences in linkage disequilibrium, allele frequency spectra, and imputation quality can alter fine-mapping resolution and effect-size transferability across groups ref [88], ref [75]. As a result, nominal replication failures may reflect population-genetic mismatch rather than true absence of effect.

These issues complicate biological interpretation and clinical translation. Studies that pool ancestries without careful modeling risk confounding, whereas studies that exclude non-European participants sacrifice generalizability and can worsen disparities in downstream prediction. Progress therefore depends on better representation of diverse populations, ancestry-aware statistical methods, and transparent reporting of recruitment, genetic ancestry inference, and cross-ancestry performance ref [75], ref [89].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Limitations and Sources of Inconsistency
subsections.subsection_title: Multiple testing and weak replication standards
subsections.content:
A persistent source of inconsistency has been the large multiplicity burden inherent in high-dimensional association studies. Early candidate-gene work often tested many variants, phenotypic definitions, and subgroup models without adequately correcting the family-wise error rate, creating a literature enriched for nominally significant but non-robust findings. The broader genetics literature has repeatedly shown that underpowered studies combined with flexible analytic choices inflate false-positive rates and exaggerate effect sizes, especially when significance thresholds are lenient or inconsistently applied ref [90], ref [91].

Replication standards have also often been weak. Claims based on same-sample internal split testing, partially overlapping cohorts, or replication at nominal rather than field-appropriate thresholds provide limited protection against chance findings. Ioannidis argued more generally that low prior probabilities, selective analysis, and researcher degrees of freedom make many published associations unlikely to be true ref [81]. In complex trait genetics, the move toward stringent genome-wide thresholds and large independent consortia emerged precisely because most early reported associations did not replicate reliably ref [92].

For this field, the implication is that isolated positive findings should be interpreted cautiously unless they survive explicit correction for multiple comparisons, are reproduced in fully independent samples, and show concordant direction and magnitude of effect. More rigorous calibration of significance and replication would reduce spurious heterogeneity and improve the evidential value of reported associations ref [91], ref [93].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Limitations and Sources of Inconsistency
subsections.content:
A persistent source of inconsistency is that many associations are estimated in clinically heterogeneous samples in which the target phenotype co-occurs with other psychiatric, metabolic, or behavioral conditions. Such comorbidity can inflate, attenuate, or even reverse apparent effects when shared liability is mistaken for disorder-specific signal. Genomic analyses have repeatedly shown substantial cross-disorder overlap, implying that findings attributed to a single diagnosis may partly reflect broader psychopathology dimensions rather than disease-specific mechanisms ref [94], ref [95].

Confounding further complicates interpretation because measured associations may be induced by socioeconomic position, medication exposure, lifestyle, population structure, or family-level environmental factors. In psychiatric and behavioral genetics especially, genetic correlations can arise through pleiotropy but also through mediated pathways and environmental stratification. Family-based analyses have shown that part of the predictive signal captured by polygenic scores reflects indirect genetic effects and demographic confounding rather than direct biological liability, underscoring the difficulty of attributing observed effects to individual-level causal mechanisms ref [96].

These issues create profound causal ambiguity. Standard case-control or cross-sectional designs are poorly suited to distinguish cause from consequence, prodrome from correlate, or shared risk factor from downstream effect. Methodological frameworks such as Mendelian randomization can strengthen causal inference, but they remain vulnerable to horizontal pleiotropy, dynastic effects, and selection bias when their assumptions are violated ref [97]. More rigorous phenotyping, longitudinal sampling, within-family designs, and explicit modeling of correlated traits are therefore essential for disentangling comorbidity from causation.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Limitations and Sources of Inconsistency
subsections.subsection_title: Publication bias and heterogeneity in effect estimates
subsections.content:
Publication bias has likely inflated the early literature, especially when nominally significant associations from small, underpowered studies were preferentially reported and interpreted as biologically meaningful. Across biomedical research, Ioannidis argued that low prior probabilities, flexible analyses, and selective reporting make many published findings vulnerable to overstatement or non-replication, a concern that applies directly to association studies with modest effect sizes ref [81]. In genetics more specifically, the “winner’s curse” further exaggerates initial effect estimates, so early positive reports often appear stronger than later, better-powered replications ref [98].

Substantial heterogeneity in effect estimates also arises from differences in phenotype definition, ascertainment, ancestry composition, covariate adjustment, and measurement platforms. These sources of between-study variation can produce inconsistent direction or magnitude of effects even when a signal is genuine, and they complicate interpretation of meta-analytic summaries. Random-effects meta-analysis is often used to accommodate such variability, but the approach can yield unstable pooled estimates when the number of studies is small or when heterogeneity is extreme ref [99].

These problems have practical consequences for translation. Inflated or highly variable effect sizes undermine confidence in biological inference, reduce the calibration of downstream risk models, and make the literature appear more contradictory than it may truly be. Large collaborative consortia, preregistered analytic plans, transparent reporting of null findings, and replication in independent datasets are therefore essential for distinguishing true but context-dependent effects from artifacts of selective publication and sampling variability ref [100].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Limitations and Sources of Inconsistency
subsections.content:
Despite rapid growth in genomic discovery, current predictive models remain limited in clinical utility. For most complex traits and psychiatric outcomes, polygenic scores explain only a modest fraction of variance, and discrimination is often insufficient for screening or individual-level decision-making. Even when statistically significant, gains over simple demographic or family-history models are frequently small, underscoring the gap between association signal and actionable prediction ref [101], ref [75].

A central limitation is poor transportability across cohorts and especially across ancestry groups. Scores derived primarily from European-ancestry discovery samples typically lose substantial accuracy in non-European populations because of differences in linkage disequilibrium, allele frequencies, environmental context, and phenotype definition. This constrains both equity and generalizability, and implies that reported performance in discovery-matched samples can substantially overstate real-world utility ref [88], ref [102].

Predictive performance is also often inflated by methodological choices, including sample overlap between discovery and target sets, overfitting during model tuning, and selective reporting of the best-performing threshold or algorithm. Moreover, standard metrics such as incremental R2 or AUC may obscure poor calibration and limited usefulness at clinically relevant decision thresholds. Recent evaluations therefore argue that stronger external validation, ancestry-diverse training data, and explicit benchmarking against established clinical predictors are necessary before routine implementation can be justified ref [75], ref [103].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Integrative, Ethical, and Translational Horizons
subsections.subsection_title: Larger consortia and harmonized international datasets
subsections.content:
Progress in psychiatric genetics has made clear that discovery for suicidal thoughts and behaviors will depend on substantially larger, better harmonized samples than have typically been available in single cohorts. Early genome-wide studies of suicide attempt and suicide death were underpowered and often relied on heterogeneous ascertainment, limiting reproducibility and cross-study comparability. The emergence of large collaborative efforts has begun to change this landscape by demonstrating that clinically meaningful loci and polygenic signal can be detected when sample sizes increase and meta-analytic coordination improves ref [9], ref [29].

A central next step is international harmonization of phenotypes, including clearer separation of suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, and suicide death; standardized definitions of lethality, intent, and recurrence; and transparent documentation of assessment context. Experience from cross-consortium analyses in psychiatry shows that broad genomic sharing can be combined with careful phenotype mapping and quality control, enabling robust trans-ancestry and cross-disorder inference ref [104], ref [74]. For suicidology, this will likely require federated collaborations linking biobanks, electronic health records, psychological autopsy studies, and population registries, while preserving the ability to model setting-specific risk factors.

Larger consortia should also prioritize inclusion of understudied populations and linkage to longitudinal environmental and treatment data. Population-wide registers and national biobanks illustrate the power of integrating genomic data with prospective health records for rare but severe outcomes such as suicidal behavior ref [25]. Ultimately, harmonized international datasets will be most valuable when they support not only gene discovery, but also calibration, replication, and equitable generalization across health systems, ancestries, and developmental stages.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Integrative, Ethical, and Translational Horizons
subsections.content:
A key next step is to move beyond single-layer association signals toward integrated models that connect common variant risk for suicidal thoughts and behaviors to molecular mechanisms across tissues, cell types, and developmental windows. Psychiatric genomics has already shown the value of coupling GWAS with transcriptomic and epigenomic resources to prioritize biologically plausible genes and pathways, particularly through brain expression quantitative trait loci, chromatin annotations, and gene-network approaches ref [80], ref [105]. For suicidal behavior, such strategies could help distinguish liability shared with depression, impulsivity, and substance use from mechanisms more proximal to stress responsivity, synaptic plasticity, and neuroimmune signaling.

Multi-omic integration should also leverage peripheral and postmortem datasets, while recognizing their distinct inferential limits. Transcriptomic studies of suicide death have repeatedly implicated altered immune and glial pathways and dysregulated cortical gene expression, suggesting that systems-level signatures may emerge more clearly than single-gene effects ref [106], ref [107]. Network-based methods, including co-expression modules and transcriptome-wide association analyses, can therefore be especially useful for identifying convergent biology from modestly powered datasets and for linking inherited risk to downstream molecular states.

The field will benefit most from designs that jointly model genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and environmental exposures in longitudinal cohorts. Integrative frameworks such as eQTL-informed fine-mapping and transcriptome imputation offer a template for prioritizing causal mechanisms ref [108], but suicide research will require careful harmonization of phenotype definitions, medication and trauma histories, and ancestry-specific molecular reference panels. Ultimately, a systems biology perspective may clarify which molecular alterations index enduring vulnerability, acute crisis states, or consequences of self-harm and treatment.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Integrative, Ethical, and Translational Horizons
subsections.content:
Future work on suicidal behavior should move beyond static main-effect models to explicitly test how genetic liability is moderated by environmental exposures across development. Twin and family studies have long suggested that the relative contribution of genetic and environmental influences on suicidal thoughts and behaviors is not constant, but varies with age, psychiatric comorbidity, and exposure to adversity ref [31]. In parallel, developmental psychopathology frameworks emphasize that risk unfolds through cascades linking early temperament, family context, trauma, substance use, and emerging psychopathology, implying that genomic studies will be most informative when anchored to longitudinal designs rather than cross-sectional case-control contrasts.

A central priority is therefore to integrate polygenic liability with well-measured exposures such as childhood maltreatment, bullying, discrimination, sleep disruption, and acute stressors. Prospective cohort data indicate that childhood adversity is one of the most robust distal predictors of later suicide attempt, while exposure to stressful life events may precipitate transitions from ideation to action ref [109], ref [110]. These observations argue for models that distinguish genetic contributions to broad liability from environmentally contingent mechanisms affecting timing, persistence, and escalation of suicidal phenomena.

Developmentally informed gene-environment research should also incorporate biological embedding. Reviews of epigenetic work have highlighted stress-responsive pathways, including glucocorticoid signaling and immune-related processes, as plausible mediators linking adversity to later suicidal behavior, although findings remain heterogeneous and underpowered ref [111]. Large longitudinal cohorts with repeated environmental, clinical, and multi-omic measures will be essential to test sensitive periods, mediation, and reciprocal effects, while reducing recall bias and strengthening causal inference ref [112].

Methodologically, the field will benefit from quasi-experimental designs, within-family analyses, and harmonized exposure measures that can separate correlation from interaction and account for gene-environment correlation. Such approaches may clarify whether genomic risk amplifies sensitivity to adversity, shapes selection into high-risk environments, or primarily acts through intermediate traits such as impulsivity, depression, and stress reactivity.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Integrative, Ethical, and Translational Horizons
subsections.subsection_title: Ancestral diversity and equity in psychiatric genetics
subsections.content:
A central limitation of psychiatric genetics, including studies of suicidal thoughts and behaviors, is the overwhelming predominance of European-ancestry cohorts. This imbalance reduces discovery in globally representative populations and weakens the portability of genetic findings, especially polygenic scores, across ancestries. Reviews of psychiatric genomics have emphasized that underrepresentation is not merely a technical issue but a source of systematic inequity in who benefits from genomic research and eventual clinical translation ref [113], ref [114].

For suicidal behavior, improving ancestral diversity is especially important because genetic liability is likely to interact with culturally patterned exposures, structural adversity, trauma burden, and differences in help-seeking and ascertainment. Empirical work across complex traits has shown that polygenic prediction accuracy declines substantially when scores derived from European discovery samples are applied to non-European populations, owing to differences in linkage disequilibrium, allele frequencies, and environmental context ref [75]. Thus, equitable progress will require larger multi-ancestry consortia, ancestry-aware fine-mapping, and harmonized phenotyping that remains sensitive to local meanings of self-harm, suicide attempt, and related outcomes.

Equity also demands attention to community partnership, governance, and the prevention of stigma. Frameworks emerging from global genomic ethics argue that inclusion should involve reciprocal benefit, transparent consent, and respect for population-specific concerns rather than simple sample extraction ref [115]. In practice, future studies of suicidal behavior should prioritize capacity building in underrepresented settings, careful interpretation of ancestry-associated findings, and dissemination strategies that avoid reifying racial categories while still addressing real disparities in risk, care access, and research representation.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Integrative, Ethical, and Translational Horizons
subsections.content:
A central next step for psychiatric genetics of suicidal behavior is to move from statistical association to causal mechanism. Because most risk loci identified for psychiatric phenotypes map to noncoding regulatory regions, functional follow-up should prioritize fine-mapping, cell-type-specific regulatory annotation, and perturbational testing in relevant neural and peripheral systems. Large-scale work linking common variant architecture to gene expression and chromatin state in human brain provides a framework for this transition, but suicide-focused studies will require explicit integration with transcriptomic and epigenomic data from implicated cortico-limbic circuits and stress-responsive cell populations ref [116], ref [117].

Mechanistic validation should also exploit single-cell atlases and experimental perturbation platforms. Cell-resolved maps of the human cortex now enable risk genes to be localized to specific excitatory, inhibitory, and glial populations, helping distinguish broad psychiatric liability from pathways more proximal to impulsive aggression, affective dysregulation, or stress reactivity ref [118]. Candidate genes and regulatory elements can then be tested using CRISPR-based perturbation, induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons, brain organoids, and animal models designed around endophenotypes rather than the difficult-to-model act of suicide itself. Such work is especially important for prioritizing convergent biological processes, including synaptic signaling, neuroinflammation, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis regulation, that may link inherited liability to environmental adversity ref [119].

More broadly, functional studies should be embedded in bidirectional pipelines in which human genetic discovery informs experiments, and experimental results refine statistical models and target prioritization. This iterative strategy may help identify tractable molecular nodes for intervention while avoiding overinterpretation of polygenic findings in the absence of demonstrated biological effect.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Integrative, Ethical, and Translational Horizons
subsections.content:
Clinical translation of genetic findings on suicidal behavior should proceed cautiously and primarily as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, comprehensive clinical assessment. Current polygenic scores explain only a modest fraction of variance in psychiatric and behavioral outcomes, and their predictive performance is especially limited when transported across health systems and ancestry groups, constraining immediate utility for individual-level decision making ref [120], ref [75]. In practice, translational value may emerge first through etiologic stratification, identification of biologically relevant pathways, and integration with longitudinal clinical, environmental, and digital phenotypes rather than through stand-alone genetic risk prediction.

Ethical concerns are particularly salient because suicide-related phenotypes are highly stigmatized, developmentally dynamic, and deeply embedded in social context. Misinterpretation of probabilistic genetic findings could reinforce determinism, exacerbate stigma, or contribute to inappropriate surveillance, coercive interventions, or discriminatory uses by insurers, schools, employers, or justice systems. These risks are amplified when prediction tools are deployed without transparency, calibration across populations, or meaningful evidence of clinical benefit; broader critiques of algorithmic prediction in psychiatry underscore the need to distinguish statistical association from actionable utility ref [121].

Accordingly, translational frameworks should emphasize participatory governance, careful communication of uncertainty, protections for privacy and data sharing, and explicit evaluation of equity impacts across ancestry, age, and socioeconomic groups. Recommendations from psychiatric genetics ethics scholarship further support embedding genetic information within person-centered care, avoiding exceptional claims about predictive power, and ensuring that any implementation is accompanied by ongoing monitoring for benefit, harm, and disparate impact ref [103].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Integrative, Ethical, and Translational Horizons
subsections.content:
A precision prevention framework for suicidal behavior should move beyond static, one-time risk stratification toward dynamic models that integrate genetic liability with clinical history, environmental exposures, and proximal changes in affect and cognition. Current evidence suggests that polygenic signals for suicide attempt and related psychiatric traits may eventually contribute to multivariable prediction, but their incremental utility is likely to depend on combination with richly phenotyped longitudinal data rather than standalone genomic screening ref [9], ref [122].

In practice, prevention-oriented models will need to link distal liability to actionable time scales. Work on short-term suicide risk prediction in health systems has shown that scalable algorithms can identify high-risk periods from routinely collected data, while advances in digital phenotyping and ecological assessment offer a path for tracking within-person fluctuations that may mediate the transition from vulnerability to crisis ref [123], ref [124]. For genetics, this implies a role as one layer in adaptive risk architectures that are repeatedly updated across development and care settings.

Any precision prevention agenda must also be judged by clinical usefulness, equity, and ethical acceptability. Because predictive models can amplify disparities when trained on unrepresentative samples or deployed without attention to access and stigma, genomic information should be incorporated only with rigorous calibration across ancestries and transparent evaluation of benefit, harm, and patient preferences ref [122], ref [75]. The most credible near-term goal is therefore not deterministic prediction, but personalized prevention pathways that match monitoring intensity and intervention options to evolving, multidomain risk.
